The coelacanth, Latimeria chalumnae, is a remarkable living fossil that exhibits several distinctive life-history traits. Newborn individuals emerge from the female's reproductive tract at a total length of 36 centimeters [Lb = 36 centimeters], a relatively large size for a marine fish that reflects an extended period of intrauterine development. Field studies conducted off the coasts of the Comoros Islands and South Africa have provided valuable data on the species' growth patterns and maximum body dimensions. The ultimate total length recorded for adult females reaches 199 centimeters [Li = 199 centimeters], while males attain a somewhat smaller maximum length of 168 centimeters [Li = 168 centimeters], indicating a moderate degree of sexual size dimorphism that likely influences reproductive behavior and partitioning of ecological resources within the deep-water reef habitats the species occupies.

Sexual maturation in Latimeria chalumnae occurs relatively late compared to most teleost fishes, aligning with its slow-paced life history. The length at which individuals attain puberty has been estimated at 150 centimeters [Lp = 150 centimeters] in total body length, a size that represents a substantial proportion of the species' ultimate length. Under the ambient thermal conditions typical of its deep-water environment, consistently recorded at 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the age at which females first give birth has been calculated at approximately 427 days [ab = approximately 427 days], a surprising figure that reflects an unusual reproductive strategy involving internal fertilization and the retention of developing young. This gestation period, accompanied by the production of a modest number of fully developed offspring, is characteristic of a life history where every reproductive event demands substantial maternal investment.

The maximum reproductive rate of the coelacanth is constrained by its lengthy gestation and the small litter sizes documented in the scientific literature. Reports indicate that females produce between 5 and 25 pups per clutch [N_R_i = between 5 and 25 pups per clutch], and given that parturition occurs approximately once every 427 days, this yields an annual reproductive frequency of roughly 0.85 clutches per year [F_R_i = roughly 0.85 clutches per year]. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 80,000 grams [Wwi = 80,000 grams], making them among the heaviest bony fishes inhabiting continental slope environments, though this maximum recorded body mass appears to be achieved only after many decades of growth.

Longevity is another hallmark of this species' extreme life-history strategy, with the maximum lifespan documented at 17,520 days [am = 17,520 days] under the consistent thermal conditions of 14 °C [T = 14 °C] that prevail in its deep-sea habitat. This exceptional duration places the coelacanth among the most long-lived vertebrate species known to science. The combination of such an extended lifespan with a low annual reproductive output and late maturation is consistent with a slow pace-of-life syndrome. The age at first reproduction, which represents the point when a female first produces a viable litter, occurs at approximately 5,840 days after birth [tR = approximately 5,840 days after birth], an interval that corresponds to roughly 16 years, a remarkably late onset of breeding even for a long-lived marine vertebrate at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C].

A prolonged juvenile phase characterizes the development of this species, during which individuals must accumulate substantial body mass before initiating reproductive activity. The ultimate wet weight of 80,000 grams [Wwi = 80,000 grams] is attained only after many years of feeding on a diet of cephalopods and benthic fishes in the mesopelagic zone. The thermal environment of the coelacanth at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] is remarkably stable throughout its depth range, and this constant cool temperature is thought to be a primary driver of its extremely slow growth, late maturity, and exceptional longevity relative to other teleosts inhabiting warmer surface waters. The coelacanth's deep-water lifestyle and conservative life-history strategy represent a distinctive evolutionary trajectory among Sarcopterygii.
